items.stem: A firm maximises profit at the output where
options: total revenue is at a maximum
average cost is at a minimum
marginal cost equals marginal revenue and MC is rising
items.answer: marginal cost equals marginal revenue and MC is rising
items.markingKey: MC = MR (with MC cutting MR from below).

items.stem: Explain why profit is maximised where marginal cost equals marginal revenue.
items.answer: If MR > MC, producing one more unit adds to profit, so output should rise; if MC > MR, the last unit reduces profit, so output should fall. Profit stops increasing only where MC = MR.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MR > MC → expand; 1 mark: MC > MR → contract; 1 mark: MC = MR maximum [3]

items.stem: Explain why a firm might find it difficult to apply the MC = MR rule in practice.
items.answer: Firms rarely know their marginal cost and marginal revenue precisely; demand is uncertain and rivals react; firms often use cost-plus pricing instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total revenue ($): 74, 136, 186, 224, 250, 264, 266; Total cost ($): 58, 72, 90, 120, 170, 248, 362. At which output does the firm maximise profit?
items.answer: 4 units
items.markingKey: Profit = TR − TC: 16, 64, 96, 104, 80, 16, -96; maximum $104 at 4 units.

items.stem: A firm’s revenue and costs are shown. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total revenue ($): 74, 136, 186, 224, 250, 264, 266; Total cost ($): 94, 106, 120, 140, 170, 214, 276. (a) Calculate marginal revenue and marginal cost for each unit. (b) Use the MC = MR rule to identify the profit-maximising output and calculate the profit.
items.markingKey: (a) MR = ΔTR, MC = ΔTC [2]; (b) produce while MR ≥ MC [1]; profit = TR − TC at that output [1].

items.stem: A firm’s revenue and costs are shown. Output: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; Total revenue ($): 75, 140, 195, 240, 275, 300, 315; Total cost ($): 103, 123, 146, 178, 225, 293, 388. (a) Calculate marginal revenue and marginal cost for each unit. (b) Use the MC = MR rule to identify the profit-maximising output and calculate the profit. (c) Explain why producing one more unit would reduce profit.
items.answer: (a) MR: 75, 65, 55, 45, 35, 25, 15; MC: 23, 20, 23, 32, 47, 68, 95 (b) 4 units: last unit with MR ≥ MC; profit = $62. (c) Unit 5 has MR $35 but MC $47, so it adds more to cost than to revenue.
items.markingKey: (a) MR = ΔTR, MC = ΔTC [2]; (b) produce while MR ≥ MC [1]; profit = TR − TC at that output [1]. (c) MC > MR for the next unit [1].

items.stem: Extract: Shareholders of Granite Holdings, a publishing company in Kestria, complain that its profit margin has fallen from 12% to 10% in three years while sales revenue grew by 30%. Senior managers receive bonuses based on market share. (a) Explain what is meant by the divorce of ownership and control. (b) Explain why the managers may have pursued sales growth rather than profit.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders own the firm but salaried managers control day-to-day decisions. (b) Bonuses linked to market share; status and power from a larger firm; principal–agent problem.

items.stem: Extract: Shareholders of Fenwick & Co, an electricity supply company in Dravonia, complain that its profit margin has fallen from 15% to 10% in three years while sales revenue grew by 25%. Senior managers receive bonuses based on market share. (a) With the aid of a diagram, compare the outputs of a profit-maximising firm and a sales-maximising firm. (b) Calculate the percentage change in the profit margin.
items.answer: (a) Profit max where MC = MR; sales max where AR = AC: higher output, lower price, normal profit only. (b) -33.3%

items.stem: If marginal revenue is greater than marginal cost, a profit-maximising firm should
items.answer: increase output
items.markingKey: Each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost.

items.stem: Redwood Corp, a producer of cement, sees its marginal cost rise because of higher energy prices while demand is unchanged. Explain the effect on its profit-maximising price and output.
items.answer: MC shifts upwards, so MC = MR occurs at a lower output; with a downward-sloping demand curve the price read from AR rises.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC shifts up, new MC = MR at lower Q; 1 mark: higher price [2]

items.stem: Ironleaf finds that the marginal revenue from its last batch of printed newspapers was $8,000 while the marginal cost was $9,500. Explain what it should do to increase profit.
items.answer: MC > MR, so the last batch reduced profit by $1,500. It should cut output until MC = MR.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC > MR reduces profit; 1 mark: reduce output to MC = MR [2]

items.markingKey: 1 mark: MC shifts up, new MC = MR at lower Q; 1 mark: higher price [2]

items.stem: Juniper Brands has announced that it will cut prices to increase its market share in Gorvania. (a) With the aid of a diagram, explain why profit is maximised where MC = MR. (b) Evaluate the view that all firms aim to maximise profits.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Profit maximisation explains entry/exit and pricing; shareholders demand it. (b) Case for the view: Profit maximisation explains entry/exit and pricing; shareholders demand it. Case against / evaluation: Alternative objectives: survival, sales/revenue, satisficing, social enterprises, managers’ goals; lack of information about MC and MR. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A firm aiming to maximise total revenue produces where
items.answer: marginal revenue is zero
items.markingKey: TR is maximised where MR = 0.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, compare the price and output of a firm that maximises profit, revenue and sales.
items.answer: Diagram: AR and MR downward sloping, MC and AC. Profit max at Q1 where MC = MR; revenue max at Q2 where MR = 0 (higher output, lower price); sales max at Q3 where AR = AC (highest output, lowest price, normal profit only). So Q1 < Q2 < Q3 and P1 > P2 > P3 (typically).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each output identified, 1 mark ordering of prices [4]

items.stem: Explain why a firm might choose to maximise revenue rather than profit.
items.answer: Managers’ pay or status may be linked to sales; a larger market share may deter entry and give future economies of scale; profit is hard to calculate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason explained [2]

The principal–agent problem in a public limited company arises because
options: managers (agents) may pursue their own objectives rather than those of shareholders (principals)
items.answer: managers (agents) may pursue their own objectives rather than those of shareholders (principals)

items.stem: Which measure is most likely to reduce the principal–agent problem?
options: Paying managers a fixed salary regardless of performance
Linking managers’ pay to the firm’s share price or profit
Reducing the number of shareholders’ meetings
items.answer: Linking managers’ pay to the firm’s share price or profit
items.markingKey: Aligning incentives, e.g. share options, profit-related bonuses.

items.stem: Explain why the divorce of ownership and control may lead firms not to maximise profits.
items.answer: Shareholders cannot monitor managers closely (asymmetric information); managers may pursue sales growth, perks or a quiet life, satisficing on profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: separation and information gap; 1 mark: alternative managerial goals [2]

items.stem: Meridian Group is a public limited company. Output (000): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; Revenue ($m): 380, 420, 520, 800, 820; Profit ($m): 20, 80, 130, 90, 30. The chief executive receives a bonus of 1% of revenue. (a) Identify the output that shareholders would prefer and the output the chief executive is likely to choose. (b) Calculate the profit lost to shareholders if the chief executive chooses this output. (c) Explain how this illustrates the principal–agent problem.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders: 30 thousand (profit $130m); chief executive: 50 thousand (highest revenue). (b) $100m. (c) The agent’s reward depends on revenue, not profit, so the manager’s choice differs from the owners’ objective; owners cannot easily monitor this.
items.markingKey: (a) profit max at 30 [1]; revenue max at 50 [1]; (b) 130 − 30 = 100 [1]; (c) principal–agent explanation with incentive mismatch [2].

items.stem: Shareholders of Pinnacle plc voted against the chief executive’s pay package this year. ‘The principal–agent problem means that large companies are run in the interests of managers rather than shareholders.’ Evaluate this statement.
items.answer: Arguments for: Managers have information advantages and their own goals. Arguments against / evaluation: Incentive schemes, takeover threats, institutional investors and corporate governance reduce the problem; managers’ goals may align with long-run profit. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Explain one problem with linking managers’ bonuses to short-term profits.

items.stem: During a recession, Cobalt Group cut prices to cover only its variable costs. Explain why survival may be its main objective.
items.answer: With falling demand it must keep cash flowing and customers loyal; covering variable costs keeps it trading until conditions improve.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: survival definition; 1 mark: application [2]

items.stem: A firm faces demand P = 50 − 1Q (MR = 50 − 2Q). Its total cost is TC = 364 + 10Q, so MC = 10 and AC = 364/Q + 10. Calculate the output that maximises profit.
items.answer: 20 units

items.stem: A firm faces demand P = 48 − 1Q (MR = 48 − 2Q). Its total cost is TC = 288 + 12Q, so MC = 12 and AC = 288/Q + 12. Calculate the output that maximises profit.
items.answer: 18 units

items.stem: Extract: Shareholders of Meridian Group, a rail transport company in Loristan, complain that its profit margin has fallen from 18% to 8% in three years while sales revenue grew by 25%. Senior managers receive bonuses based on market share. (a) Explain what is meant by the divorce of ownership and control. (b) Explain why the managers may have pursued sales growth rather than profit.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders own the firm but salaried managers control day-to-day decisions. (b) Bonuses linked to market share; status and power from a larger firm; principal–agent problem.

items.stem: In the principal–agent relationship between a patient and a doctor, the agent is
items.answer: the doctor
items.markingKey: The agent acts on behalf of the principal and has more information.

items.stem: Shareholders of Delta Foods complain that managers have spent heavily on luxury offices and company jets. Explain how this illustrates the principal–agent problem.
items.answer: Managers (agents) use company resources for their own benefit rather than to maximise shareholders’ (principals’) profit; dispersed shareholders cannot monitor closely.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identify principals and agents; 1 mark: conflicting objectives/information [2]

items.stem: Tidewater plc is a public limited company. Output (000): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; Revenue ($m): 200, 240, 300, 340, 460; Profit ($m): 60, 100, 150, 90, 50. The chief executive receives a bonus of 0.5% of revenue. (a) Identify the output that shareholders would prefer and the output the chief executive is likely to choose. (b) Calculate the profit lost to shareholders if the chief executive chooses this output. (c) Explain how this illustrates the principal–agent problem.
items.answer: (a) Shareholders: 30 thousand (profit $150m); chief executive: 50 thousand (highest revenue). (b) $100m. (c) The agent’s reward depends on revenue, not profit, so the manager’s choice differs from the owners’ objective; owners cannot easily monitor this.
items.markingKey: (a) profit max at 30 [1]; revenue max at 50 [1]; (b) 150 − 50 = 100 [1]; (c) principal–agent explanation with incentive mismatch [2].

items.stem: Extract: Shareholders of Horizon Corp, a cement company in Jovania, complain that its profit margin has fallen from 15% to 8% in three years while sales revenue grew by 30%. Senior managers receive bonuses based on market share. (a) Explain why the managers may have pursued sales growth rather than profit. (b) Discuss how shareholders might ensure that managers act in their interests.
items.answer: (a) Bonuses linked to market share; status and power from a larger firm; principal–agent problem. (b) Share options, profit-related pay, non-executive directors, voting at AGMs, threat of takeover; limitations: short-termism, information gaps.
